literal: Duke of Shanggu Heluo was a great-grandson of Emperor Shenyuan.
idiomatic: Heluo, Duke of Shanggu, was a great-grandson of Emperor Shenyuan.

literal: At first he followed Taizu from the Dugu clan to the Helan tribe, gathered old households, and obtained three hundred families; with his younger brother Jian he proposed urging Henai to elevate Taizu as chief.
idiomatic: Early on he followed Taizu from the Dugu to the Helan, rallied three hundred old households, and with his brother Jian urged Henai to make Taizu their leader.

literal: When Taizu ascended the royal throne, Heluo constantly guarded close at his left and right.
idiomatic: After Taizu took the kingship, Heluo served constantly at his side.

literal: He also followed on campaigns and had great merit.
idiomatic: He campaigned as well and won great distinction.

literal: Heluo had merit in the plan to support enthronement and was especially favored and rewarded.
idiomatic: Because Heluo had helped raise Taizu to power, he received exceptional favor.

literal: When he took the imperial throne, he and his younger brother Jian were enfeoffed as dukes on the same day.
idiomatic: When Taizu became emperor, he enfeoffed Heluo and Jian as dukes on the same day.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: His son Ti was known from youth for martial prowess and was granted the title Duke of Xiangcheng.
idiomatic: His son Ti won early fame for valor and was made Duke of Xiangcheng.

literal: On the campaign against Zhongshan he received orders to march through the commanderies below, pacify Xincheng, and all were settled and glad in their work.
idiomatic: On the Zhongshan campaign he was ordered to sweep the lower commanderies; he pacified Xincheng, and the people settled gladly to their trades.

literal: His title was advanced to prince.
idiomatic: He was promoted to prince.

literal: He attacked Murong Lin at Yitai, was struck by a flying arrow, and died.
idiomatic: He fought Murong Lin at Yitai, took an arrow in flight, and died.

literal: The emperor, because Grand Physician Yin Guang's treatment did not exhaust every art, had him executed.
idiomatic: The emperor held that Grand Physician Yin Guang had not done all he could and had him put to death.

literal: His son Xiji succeeded; the title was reduced to Duke of Xiangcheng.
idiomatic: His son Xiji inherited the line but was demoted to Duke of Xiangcheng.

literal: He died; posthumously he was made Prince of Xiangcheng.
idiomatic: When he died he was posthumously made Prince of Xiangcheng.

literal: Duke of Jiande Yingwen was a descendant of Emperor Shenyuan.
idiomatic: Yingwen, Duke of Jiande, descended from Emperor Shenyuan.

literal: From youth he was clear in debate and decisive; Emperor Taizong valued him.
idiomatic: Clever and resolute from youth, he won Emperor Taizong's esteem.

literal: He managed outgoing and incoming edicts and orders and often held confidential matters.
idiomatic: He oversaw the issuing and receipt of edicts and routinely held the keys of state.

literal: When Shizu took the throne, he was appointed Protector of the Eastern Yi, advanced to Duke of Jiande, and stationed at Liaoxi.
idiomatic: At Shizu's accession he became Protector of the Eastern Yi, was raised to Duke of Jiande, and garrisoned Liaoxi.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died in office.

literal: Marquis of Zhending Lu was a descendant of Emperor Shenyuan.
idiomatic: Lu, Marquis of Zhending, was of Emperor Shenyuan's line.

literal: In Shizu's time, for martial merit he often received favor, was made scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary, and was granted Marquis of Zhending.
idiomatic: Under Shizu his battlefield service won repeated favor: he became scattered cavalier attendant-in-ordinary and Marquis of Zhending.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: Lu's great-grandson Gui, styled Faji, gradually rose to magistrate of Luoyang.
idiomatic: Lu's great-grandson Gui, styled Faji, rose step by step to magistrate of Luoyang.

literal: When the realm had many troubles, Gui treated subordinates only with harsh severity; deaths from cruel excess were many, and the knowing disapproved.
idiomatic: In troubled times Gui ruled his subordinates with pitiless severity; many died from his excesses, and men of judgment condemned him.

literal: In Emperor Xiaojing's time, when the Ye palace was first built, Gui was made commissioner of construction.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Xiaojing, when the Ye palace was first laid out, Gui was put in charge of building it.

literal: He was removed and made Inspector of Xuzhou.
idiomatic: He was transferred to Inspector of Xuzhou.

literal: Gui's reputation was already mean and he lacked learning; though he held famous posts, men of the time looked down on him.
idiomatic: Gui's standing was already low and he had no scholarship; for all his grand titles, his contemporaries held him cheap.

literal: He died in the province.
idiomatic: He died while serving in the province.

literal: Marquis of Wuling Yin was a descendant of Emperor Zhang.
idiomatic: Yin, Marquis of Wuling, came down from Emperor Zhang.

literal: He followed Taizu in pacifying the Central Plain and for merit was enfeoffed Marquis of Quni.
idiomatic: He followed Taizu in pacifying the Central Plain and was enfeoffed Marquis of Quni for his service.

literal: In Shizu's time the title was changed to Wuling.
idiomatic: Under Shizu his fief was changed to Wuling.

literal: Prince of Changle Shoule was a descendant of Emperor Zhang.
idiomatic: Shoule, Prince of Changle, was of Emperor Zhang's line.

literal: He held office as Minister of the Selection Bureau, Prince of Nan'an, and was changed in enfeoffment to Prince of Changle.
idiomatic: He served as Minister of the Selection Bureau and Prince of Nan'an before his fief was changed to Changle.

literal: When Emperor Gaozong took the throne, Shoule had merit in supporting enthronement and was appointed Grand Preceptor, grand commander, commander of all armies within and without, and recorder of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: At Gaozong's accession Shoule was rewarded for helping put him on the throne with Grand Preceptor, grand commander, command of all armies within and without, and the post of recorder of the Masters of Writing.

literal: He boasted of merit, struggled for power with Masters of Writing Chief Zhangsun Kehou, and both were executed.
idiomatic: He grew proud of his service and wrestled for power with Chief of the Masters of Writing Zhangsun Kehou; both men were executed.

literal: Duke of Wangdu Tui was a descendant of Emperor Zhao.
idiomatic: Tui, Duke of Wangdu, descended from Emperor Zhao.

literal: He followed Taizu in pacifying the Central Plain and was granted Marquis of Wangdu.
idiomatic: He followed Taizu in pacifying the Central Plain and received Marquis of Wangdu.

literal: Shizu, because Tui's appearance was handsome and his bearing admirable, had him welcome the Left Esteemed Consort from the Ruru and advanced his title to duke.
idiomatic: Shizu thought Tui handsome and dignified in bearing and sent him to fetch the Left Esteemed Consort from the Ruru; his title was raised to duke.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He passed away.

literal: Marquis of Quyang Suyan was a descendant of Emperor Huan.
idiomatic: Suyan, Marquis of Quyang, was of Emperor Huan's line.

literal: As a petty commander he followed Taizu in campaigns against the tribes; when Bing province was first pacified he was made inspector.
idiomatic: He began as a petty commander under Taizu in tribal campaigns; when Bing was first pacified he became its inspector.

literal: When Taizu was alarmed at Baixi, Bing province's defending general Feng Douzhen rebelled and Suyan beheaded him.
idiomatic: When Taizu was thrown into alarm at Baixi, the Bing garrison commander Feng Douzhen turned rebel and Suyan cut off his head.

literal: At that time Taizu wished to soothe and please the newly attached and regretted the massacre at Canhe, but Suyan's slaughter was excessive and he was dismissed from office for the offense.
idiomatic: Taizu then meant to win over the newly submitted and regretted the slaughter at Canhe, yet Suyan had killed far too many and was removed from office.

literal: When Zhongshan was pacified, he was appointed Inspector of You province.
idiomatic: After Zhongshan fell he was made Inspector of You.

literal: Extravagant and dissolute, he was demoted to Administrator of Shanggu.
idiomatic: Luxurious and unrestrained, he was demoted to Administrator of Shanggu.

literal: Later he was granted title Marquis of Quyang.
idiomatic: Later he was enfeoffed Marquis of Quyang.

literal: At that time Taizu attended to Huang-Lao, wishing to purify custom by a simple wind; even carriage robes and trappings shed carving and ornament, all honoring plain frugality, while Suyan's luxury exceeded bounds and Taizu deeply harbored resentment.
idiomatic: Taizu then turned to Huang-Lao, hoping to refine the people through plain ways: even imperial carriages and robes lost their ornament, yet Suyan's extravagance went beyond measure, and Taizu nursed a deep grudge.

literal: Accumulating his offenses, he was summoned and sentenced to death by imperial gift.
idiomatic: When his faults piled high he was summoned and granted death.

literal: Duke of Shunyang Yu was a descendant of Emperor Huan.
idiomatic: Yu, Duke of Shunyang, came down from Emperor Huan.

literal: From youth he was loyal, upright, and unbending.
idiomatic: From boyhood he was loyal, upright, and unyielding.

literal: At first, as palace guard central cadet, he served within the palace; diligent and capable, he had a reputation.
idiomatic: He first entered service as a palace-guard cadet within the inner quarters, where diligence won him a name.

literal: In Gaozong's time he held office as Director of the Palace Secretariat.
idiomatic: Under Gaozong he became Director of the Palace Secretariat.

literal: He followed Gaozong on an eastern tour to the coast; for labor he was granted Duke of Shunyang.
idiomatic: He accompanied Gaozong on an eastern tour to the sea and, for his exertions, was made Duke of Shunyang.

literal: When Gaozong died, Yifu Hun monopolized power and cut off inside from outside; the hundred officials were shaken and fearful and could find no plan.
idiomatic: After Gaozong's death Yifu Hun seized power, sealing court from capital; officials trembled and knew no remedy.

literal: Yu led several hundred palace guards in through Shunde Gate intending to kill Hun.
idiomatic: Yu led several hundred palace guards through Shunde Gate to kill Hun.

literal: Hun was afraid, came out against him, and asked Yu, "Lord, what is your intent in entering?
idiomatic: Hun, afraid, came out to meet him and asked, "My lord, why have you entered?

literal: Yu said, "Not seeing the Son of Heaven, the ministers are anxious and fearful and seek audience with the sovereign."
idiomatic: Yu said, "We have not seen the Son of Heaven; the ministers are anxious and beg audience with their lord."

literal: Hun was distressed and afraid and said to Yu, "Now the late emperor lies in coffin and the Son of Heaven is in mourning darkness, so he has not yet received the officials—why should you lords doubt?
idiomatic: Hun, cornered and afraid, said, "The late emperor still lies in state and the Son of Heaven keeps mourning seclusion, so he has not yet received you—why this suspicion?

literal: He then presented Xianzu to hold court.
idiomatic: He then brought Xianzu out to preside at court.

literal: Later Hun's heart plotted rebellion; court ministers watched sidelong. Yu again plotted to kill Hun and was executed by Hun.
idiomatic: Later Hun turned his mind to treason and the court watched him with sidelong eyes. Yu plotted again to kill him and was slain by Hun.

literal: Xianzu recorded Yu's loyalty and rectitude, posthumously made him Prince of Shunyang, and gave posthumous title Jian.
idiomatic: Xianzu honored Yu's loyalty, posthumously raised him to Prince of Shunyang, and styled him Jian.

literal: Prince of Yidu Muchen was a descendant of Emperor Huan.
idiomatic: Muchen, Prince of Yidu, was of Emperor Huan's line.

literal: At first, as palace guard, he followed Taizu on the southern campaign as far as the Yangtze.
idiomatic: He first followed Taizu south as a palace guard, campaigning as far as the Yangtze.

literal: When Gaozong took the throne, for accumulated labor he was promoted attendant-in-ordinary and left vice director of the Masters of Writing and was enfeoffed Duke of Nanping.
idiomatic: At Gaozong's accession his long service won him attendant-in-ordinary, left vice director of the Masters of Writing, and the dukedom of Nanping.

literal: When Yifu Hun plotted disorder, Muchen and his elder brother Yu discussed killing Hun; the affair leaked and he was condemned, but Muchen fled in hiding and escaped.
idiomatic: When Yifu Hun rose in treason, Muchen and his brother Yu planned his death; the plot was exposed and Muchen was sentenced, but he hid and escaped.

literal: When Xianzu transmitted the throne he had merit in settling the plan.
idiomatic: When Xianzu abdicated in favor of the new emperor he had helped fix the succession.

literal: When Gaozu took the throne he was moved to Minister over the Masses, enfeoffed Prince of Yidu, removed and made Inspector of Yong province, and stationed at Chang'an.
idiomatic: At Gaozu's accession he became Minister over the Masses and Prince of Yidu, then left court to serve as Inspector of Yong and garrison Chang'an.

literal: Muchen's nature was unbending, upright, and aloof; he did not join factions, and court ministers all feared him.
idiomatic: Muchen was stiff, upright, and aloof, never joining cliques, and the court feared him.

literal: Yet he loved profit; in the province government was accomplished through bribes.
idiomatic: Yet he loved gain, and in Yong his rule ran on bribes.

literal: For a crime he was executed; his title was removed.
idiomatic: He was executed for a crime and his fief was extinguished.

literal: Emperor Mu's eldest son Liuxiu was from youth fierce and perverse.
idiomatic: Liuxiu, Emperor Mu's eldest son, was violent and unruly from childhood.

literal: In the fifth year of Emperor Mu he sent Liuxiu as vanguard with the assisting minister Wei Xiong, Fan Ban, and Jitan and others to rescue Liu Kun.
idiomatic: In Emperor Mu's fifth year he sent Liuxiu ahead with the assisting minister Wei Xiong, Fan Ban, Jitan, and others to relieve Liu Kun.

literal: The emperor personally commanded the great army as rear support.
idiomatic: The emperor himself led the main host as rear guard.

literal: Liu Can was afraid, burned the baggage trains, broke out, and fled.
idiomatic: Liu Can, in fear, burned his wagons, broke out, and fled.

literal: They loosed cavalry in pursuit and killed and wounded very many.
idiomatic: Pursuing cavalry killed and wounded a great multitude.

literal: The emperor then held a great hunt on Shouyang Mountain, displayed the flesh and hides for review, and the mountain turned red with the change.
idiomatic: The emperor then hunted on Shouyang Mountain, laid out flesh and hides for inspection, and the slopes ran red.

literal: When Emperor Huai of Jin was seized by Liu Cong, Emperor Mu sent Liuxiu and Emperor Huan's son Pugen with picked cavalry to aid Liu Kun.
idiomatic: When Jin's Emperor Huai fell into Liu Cong's hands, Emperor Mu sent Liuxiu and Emperor Huan's son Pugen with elite horsemen to help Liu Kun.

literal: At first Emperor Mu's youngest son Biyan was favored and he wished to make him successor.
idiomatic: Emperor Mu had long favored his youngest son Biyan and meant to make him heir.

literal: Liuxiu was sent out to dwell at Xincheng and his mother was demoted.
idiomatic: Liuxiu was sent to live at Xincheng and his mother was cast aside.

literal: Liuxiu had a bay dappled swift horse that went five hundred li a day; Emperor Mu wished to take it to give to Biyan.
idiomatic: Liuxiu owned a dappled bay that could run five hundred li in a day; Emperor Mu wanted it for Biyan.

literal: Later when Liuxiu came to court, Emperor Mu again ordered him to bow to Biyan; Liuxiu would not obey.
idiomatic: When Liuxiu later came to court, Emperor Mu again ordered him to bow to Biyan, and Liuxiu refused.

literal: Emperor Mu then seated Biyan on the walking palanquin he himself rode and had men guide and attend him on an outing.
idiomatic: Emperor Mu set Biyan on his own walking palanquin and sent attendants to escort him on parade.

literal: Liuxiu saw from afar and thought it was Emperor Mu; he bowed prostrate on the left of the road, but when he came near it was Biyan, and he left in shame and anger.
idiomatic: Liuxiu saw the procession from afar and, thinking it the emperor, bowed by the roadside—only to find Biyan and stalk away in shame and rage.

literal: Summoned, he did not return.
idiomatic: When summoned he would not come back.

literal: Emperor Mu was angry and led the multitude to attack him.
idiomatic: Enraged, Emperor Mu marched against him in force.

literal: The emperor's army was unfavorable; Liuxiu killed Biyan.
idiomatic: The imperial army fared badly, and Liuxiu killed Biyan.

literal: The emperor changed clothes and went incognito among the people; a low woman recognized the emperor and he suddenly died violently.
idiomatic: The emperor disguised himself among commoners; a humble woman recognized him, and he died suddenly.

literal: Pugen had first been guarding outside; hearing of the crisis he led troops to come.
idiomatic: Pugen had been holding the field; hearing of the disaster he hurried in with troops.

literal: He attacked Liuxiu and destroyed him.
idiomatic: He struck Liuxiu down and wiped him out.

literal: Baron of Jiyang Bigan was Taizu's younger clansman in the same generation.
idiomatic: Bigan, Baron of Jiyang, was Taizu's younger clansman.

literal: As Director of Palace Guards he campaigned against the Dingling of Baijian with merit and was granted Baron of Jiyang.
idiomatic: As Director of Palace Guards he campaigned against the Baijian Dingling with success and was made Baron of Jiyang.

literal: Later, as commander-in-chief of the southern route, he died in battle.
idiomatic: Later, commanding the southern army, he fell in battle.

literal: Duke of Jiangxia Lü was Taizu's younger clansman in the same generation.
idiomatic: Lü, Duke of Jiangxia, was Taizu's younger clansman.

literal: He followed Shizu in pacifying Liang province with merit, was enfeoffed Duke of Jiangxia, held office as chief official of the outer court, and was entrusted with court governance, greatly respected.
idiomatic: He followed Shizu in pacifying Liang, was made Duke of Jiangxia, headed the outer court, and was entrusted with state affairs to great honor.

literal: He died; posthumously he was made Prince of Jiangxia and buried alongside at Jinling.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously made Prince of Jiangxia, buried beside the imperial tombs at Jinling.

literal: Prince of Gaoliang Gu was the fourth son of Emperor Pingwen.
idiomatic: Gu, Prince of Gaoliang, was Emperor Pingwen's fourth son.

literal: He had many talents and arts and possessed will and strategy.
idiomatic: Gifted in many arts, he was a man of resolve and design.

literal: In the first year before Emperor Lie, the state had internal difficulty and Emperor Zhaocheng went to Xiangguo.
idiomatic: In the year before Emperor Lie's reign began, civil strife broke out and Emperor Zhaocheng went to Xiangguo.

literal: Later, when Emperor Lie was on the point of death, he left a dying charge: welcome Emperor Zhaocheng and establish him and the altars may be secure.
idiomatic: As Emperor Lie lay dying he charged them: bring Zhaocheng back and enthrone him, and the realm will be secure.

literal: When he died the ministers all thought there had newly been a great misfortune, inside and outside were not yet settled, Zhaocheng was in the south and his coming could not yet be made certain; in the interval before he arrived they feared fraud and change, and it was fit to establish the eldest as lord to calm public expectation.
idiomatic: At his death the ministers judged the realm too unsettled for a distant heir: Zhaocheng was still in the south, and until he came they feared intrigue; they argued that an elder lord should be set up at once to steady men's hearts.
